Bartenders mix drinks and serve them directly to customers or through wait staff.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Food processing equipment workers operate machinery that mixes, cooks, or processes ingredients for manufacturing food products.  Set up, start, or load food processing equipment Food and tobacco roasting, baking, and drying machine operators and tenders
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Education requirements vary for food processing equipment workers. Some typically need no formal education credential; however, others typically need a high school diploma or equivalent. Food processing equipment workers usually learn their skills through on-the-job training.   Detail oriented.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most food processing equipment workers are employed in manufacturing facilities. Because of production schedules, shift work is common and may include early mornings, evenings, or nights. Most food processing equipment workers are employed full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: food processing equipment workers.    Agricultural and food science technicians help scientists with testing and research related to plants, animals, fibers, and food and beverage products. Bakers mix ingredients according to recipes in order to make breads, pastries, and other baked goods. Butchers cut, trim, and package meat for retail sale. Cooks season and prepare foods, including soups, salads, entrees, and desserts. Food preparation workers perform a variety of tasks other than cooking, such as slicing meat and brewing coffee. Metal and plastic machine workers set up and operate equipment that cuts, shapes, and forms metal and plastic materials or pieces.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Food service managers are responsible for the daily operation of restaurants or other establishments that prepare and serve food and beverages. They direct staff to ensure that customers are satisfied with their dining experience, and they manage the business to ensure that it runs efficiently.  Hire, train, discipline, and sometimes fire employees
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Food service managers typically need a high school diploma and several years of experience in the food service industry working as a cook, waiter or waitress, or supervisor of food preparation and serving workers. Some receive additional training at a community college, technical or vocational school, culinary school, or 4-year college.   Business skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Food service managers work in restaurants, hotels, school cafeterias, and other establishments where food is prepared and served. They often work evenings, weekends, and holidays. The work is often hectic, and dealing with dissatisfied customers may be stressful.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: food service managers.    Bartenders mix drinks and serve them directly to customers or through wait staff. Chefs and head cooks oversee the daily food preparation at restaurants and other places where food is served. Lodging managers ensure that guests have a pleasant experience at an accommodations facility. They also plan, direct, or coordinate activities to ensure that the facility is efficient and profitable. Sales managers plan, direct, or coordinate the delivery of a product or service to the customer. Waiters and waitresses take orders and serve food and beverages to customers in dining establishments.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Forensic science technicians aid criminal investigations by collecting and analyzing evidence. Technicians often specialize in either crime scene or laboratory analysis.  Analyze crime scenes to determine what evidence should be collected and how crime scene technicians
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Forensic science technicians typically need a bachelor’s degree to enter the occupation. They may need on-the-job training to attain competency.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most laboratory forensic science technicians work during standard business hours. Some work extended or nonstandard hours and travel to crime scenes within their jurisdiction.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: forensic science technicians.    Biological technicians assist biological and medical scientists with tasks such as laboratory setup, data collection, and observation. Chemical technicians conduct laboratory tests to help scientists analyze the properties of materials. Chemists and materials scientists research and analyze the chemical properties of substances to develop new materials, products, or knowledge. Environmental science and protection technicians monitor the environment and investigate sources of pollution and contamination, including those affecting public health. Fire inspectors detect fire hazards, recommend prevention measures, ensure compliance with state and local fire regulations, and investigate causes of fires. Hazardous materials removal workers identify and dispose of harmful substances such as asbestos, lead, and radioactive waste. Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians perform medical laboratory tests for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of disease. Police officers protect lives and property. Detectives and criminal investigators gather facts and collect evidence of possible crimes. Private detectives and investigators gather, analyze, and report information to clients regarding legal or personal matters.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Forest and conservation workers improve the quality of forests, rangelands, and wetlands. Under the supervision of conservation scientists and foresters, they develop, maintain, and protect forests.  Plant seedlings to reforest land
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Forest and conservation workers typically need a high school diploma to enter the occupation and receive on-the-job training to attain competency.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Forest and conservation workers often work outdoors, sometimes in remote locations and in all types of weather. Most forest and conservation workers are employed full time, although part-time or seasonal work is common.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: forest and conservation workers.    Conservation scientists and foresters manage the land quality of forests, parks, rangelands, and other natural resources. Fire inspectors detect fire hazards, recommend prevention measures, ensure compliance with state and local fire regulations, and investigate causes of fires. Firefighters control and put out fires and respond to emergencies involving life, property, or the environment. Logging workers harvest forests to provide the raw material for many consumer goods and industrial products. Cartographers and photogrammetrists collect, analyze, and interpret geographic information to create and update maps and related products.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Fundraisers organize activities to raise money and other kinds of donations for an organization. They also may design promotional materials and increase awareness of an organization’s work, goals, and financial needs.  Research prospective donors Annual
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Fundraisers typically need a bachelor’s degree and strong communication and organizational skills. Employers may prefer to hire candidates who have related experience, such as from working with a nonprofit organization in an internship or as a volunteer.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Fundraisers work primarily for nonprofit organizations. They spend time in an office setting, although they also may travel to meet with prospective donors or to attend events. Most fundraisers work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: fundraisers.    Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers plan programs to generate interest in products or services. Market research analysts study consumer preferences, business conditions, and other factors to assess potential sales of a product or service. Meeting, convention, and event planners arrange all aspects of events and professional gatherings. Public relations managers direct the creation of materials that will enhance the public image of their employer or client. Fundraising managers coordinate campaigns that bring in donations for their organization. Public relations specialists create and maintain a positive public image for the clients they represent. Social and community service managers coordinate and supervise programs and organizations that support public well-being.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Funeral service workers organize and manage the details of a ceremony honoring a deceased person.  Offer counsel and comfort to families and friends of the deceased Funeral home managers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: An associate’s degree in a funeral service or mortuary science education program is the education typically required to become a funeral service worker. Most employers require applicants to be 21 years old, have at least 2 years of formal postsecondary education, have supervised training, and pass a state licensing exam.  Be 21 years old Business skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Funeral service workers are employed in funeral homes and crematories. They are often on call; irregular hours, including evenings and weekends, are common. Most work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: funeral service workers.    Administrative services and facilities managers plan, direct, and coordinate activities that help an organization run efficiently. Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers plan programs to generate interest in products or services. Human resources managers plan, coordinate, and direct the administrative functions of an organization. Physicians and surgeons diagnose and treat injuries or illnesses and address health maintenance. Psychologists study cognitive, emotional, and social processes and behavior by observing, interpreting, and recording how people relate to one another and to their environments. Social workers help people prevent and cope with problems in their everyday lives.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Gambling services workers serve customers in gambling establishments, such as casinos or racetracks. Some workers tend slot machines or deal cards. Others take bets or pay out winnings. Still others supervise or manage gambling workers and operations.  Interact with customers and make sure that they have a pleasant experience First-line supervisors of gambling services workers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Gambling jobs typically require a high school diploma or equivalent to enter. Some employers require gambling managers to have a college degree.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most gambling services workers are employed in gambling industries. Because most of these establishments are open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, employees often work nights, weekends, and holidays. Most work full time, although part-time work is common.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: gambling services workers.    Customer service representatives interact with customers to handle complaints, process orders, and answer questions. Lodging managers ensure that guests have a pleasant experience at an accommodations facility. They also plan, direct, or coordinate activities to ensure that the facility is efficient and profitable. Public relations managers direct the creation of materials that will enhance the public image of their employer or client. Fundraising managers coordinate campaigns that bring in donations for their organization. Public relations specialists create and maintain a positive public image for the clients they represent. Retail sales workers sell merchandise, spare and replacement parts, and equipment to customers. Sales managers plan, direct, or coordinate the delivery of a product or service to the customer. Security guards and gambling surveillance officers protect property from illegal activity. Financial clerks do administrative work, help customers, and carry out transactions that involve money.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: General maintenance and repair workers fix and maintain machines, mechanical equipment, and buildings. They paint, repair flooring, and work on plumbing, electrical, and air-conditioning and heating systems.  Maintain and repair machines, mechanical equipment, and buildings
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Jobs in this field typically do not require any formal education beyond high school. General maintenance and repair workers often learn their skills on the job. They start by doing simple tasks and watching and learning from skilled maintenance workers.   Customer-service skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: General maintenance and repair workers often carry out many different tasks in a single day. They could work at any number of indoor or outdoor locations. They may work inside a single building, such as a hotel or hospital, or be responsible for the maintenance of many buildings, such as those in an apartment complex or on a college campus.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: general maintenance and repair workers.    Boilermakers assemble, install, maintain, and repair boilers, closed vats, and other large vessels or containers that hold liquids and gases. Carpenters construct, repair, and install building frameworks and structures made from wood and other materials. Construction managers plan, coordinate, budget, and supervise construction projects from start to finish. Electrical and electronics installers and repairers install or repair a variety of electrical equipment. Electricians install, maintain, and repair electrical power, communications, lighting, and control systems. Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers work on heating, ventilation, cooling, and refrigeration systems. Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters install and repair piping fixtures and systems.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: General office clerks perform a variety of clerical tasks, including answering telephones, typing documents, and filing records.  Answer and transfer telephone calls or take messages
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: General office clerks typically need a high school diploma or equivalent to enter the occupation and learn their skills on the job.   Customer-service skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Although general office clerks are employed in nearly every industry, many work in schools, healthcare facilities, and government offices.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: general office clerks.    Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks compute, classify, and record data to help organizations keep complete and accurate financial records. Customer service representatives interact with customers to handle complaints, process orders, and answer questions. Information clerks perform routine clerical duties, maintain records, collect data, and provide information to customers. Material recording clerks track product information in order to keep businesses and supply chains on schedule. Receptionists do tasks such as answering phones, receiving visitors, and providing information about their organization to the public. Secretaries and administrative assistants do routine clerical and organizational tasks.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Genetic counselors assess clients’ risk for a variety of inherited conditions, such as birth defects. They review genetic test results with individuals and families and support them in making decisions based on those results. They also offer information to other healthcare providers.  Collect comprehensive family and medical histories through means such as interviews, discussions with physicians, and reviewing medical records
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Genetic counselors typically need a master’s degree in genetic counseling. Nearly all states require genetic counselors to be licensed, and licensure usually requires board certification.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Genetic counselors work primarily in hospitals, physicians’ offices, outpatient care centers, university medical centers, and diagnostic laboratories. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: genetic counselors.    Epidemiologists are public health workers who investigate patterns and causes of disease and injury. Health education specialists develop programs to teach people about conditions affecting well-being. Medical scientists conduct research aimed at improving overall human health. Marriage and family therapists diagnose and treat cognitive, behavioral, or similar disorders in the context of couples and other relationships. Physicians and surgeons diagnose and treat injuries or illnesses and address health maintenance.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Geographers study the Earth and the distribution of its land, features, and inhabitants. They research the interactions between the physical aspects of a region and the human activities within it.  Gather geographic data through field observations, maps, photographs, satellite imagery, and censuses Physical geographers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Geographers typically need at least a bachelor’s degree to enter the occupation. Some jobs require a master’s or doctoral degree.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most geographers work full time. Geographers who do fieldwork may travel to foreign countries or remote locations.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: geographers.    Anthropologists and archeologists study the origin, development, and behavior of humans. Cartographers and photogrammetrists collect, analyze, and interpret geographic information to create and update maps and related products. Economists conduct research, prepare reports, and evaluate issues related to monetary and fiscal policy. They also may collect and analyze statistical data. Geoscientists study the physical aspects of the Earth. Market research analysts study consumer preferences, business conditions, and other factors to assess potential sales of a product or service. Political scientists study the origin, development, and operation of political systems. Postsecondary teachers instruct students in a variety of academic subjects beyond the high school level. Surveying and mapping technicians collect data and make maps of the Earth's surface. Surveyors make precise measurements to determine property boundaries. Urban and regional planners develop comprehensive plans and programs for use of land and physical facilities in cities, counties, metropolitan areas, and other jurisdictions.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Geological and hydrologic technicians support scientists and engineers in exploring, extracting, and monitoring natural resources, such as soil, natural gas, and water.  Install and maintain laboratory and field equipment
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Geological and hydrologic technicians typically need at least an associate’s degree in applied science or science-related technology to enter the occupation. Some employers require a bachelor’s degree. Geological and hydrologic technicians also receive on-the-job training.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Geological and hydrologic technicians work in offices, laboratories, and the field. Most geological and hydrologic technicians work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: geological and hydrologic technicians.    Cartographers and photogrammetrists collect, analyze, and interpret geographic information to create and update maps and related products. Civil engineering technologists and technicians help civil engineers plan, design, and build infrastructure and development projects. Civil engineers plan, design, and supervise the construction and maintenance of building and infrastructure projects. Geoscientists study the physical aspects of the Earth. Hydrologists study water and how it moves across and through the Earth’s crust. Petroleum engineers devise methods to improve oil and gas extraction and production. Surveying and mapping technicians collect data and make maps of the Earth's surface.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Geoscientists study the physical aspects of the Earth, such as its composition, structure, and processes, to learn about its past and present and to predict future events.  Plan and carry out field studies, in which they visit locations to collect samples and conduct surveys Environmental
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Geoscientists typically need a bachelor’s degree to enter the occupation. For some positions, employers prefer to hire candidates who have a master’s or doctoral degree. Most geoscientists need a state-issued license.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Geoscientists usually split their time between work in an office setting, in laboratories, and outdoors. Most geoscientists work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week. Schedules vary to include irregular hours when doing fieldwork.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: geoscientists.    Anthropologists and archeologists study the origin, development, and behavior of humans. Atmospheric scientists study, report on, and forecast the weather and climate. Environmental engineers use engineering disciplines in developing solutions to problems of planetary health. Environmental scientists and specialists conduct research or investigations to protect the environment or human health. Geological and hydrologic technicians support scientists and engineers in exploring, extracting, and monitoring natural resources. Hydrologists study water and how it moves across and through the Earth’s crust. Mining and geological engineers design mines to safely and efficiently remove minerals for use in manufacturing and utilities. Natural sciences managers plan, supervise, or coordinate research and other activities in fields such as life sciences, physical sciences, mathematics, and statistics. Physicists and astronomers study the interactions of matter and energy. Petroleum engineers devise methods to improve oil and gas extraction and production.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Glaziers install glass in windows, skylights, and other fixtures in buildings.  Follow blueprints and specifications
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Glaziers typically enter the occupation with a high school diploma and learn their trade through an apprenticeship or on-the-job training.   Ability to work at heights.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: As in many other construction trades, the work of glaziers is physically demanding. They may experience cuts from tools and glass, falls from ladders and scaffolding, and exposure to solvents. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: glaziers.    Automotive body and glass repairers restore, refinish, and replace vehicle bodies and frames, windshields, and window glass. Carpenters construct, repair, and install building frameworks and structures made from wood and other materials. Construction laborers and helpers perform tasks, such as using, supplying, or holding materials or tools and cleaning work areas and equipment, on construction sites. Drywall and ceiling tile installers hang wallboard and install ceiling tile inside buildings. Tapers prepare the wallboard for painting. Masonry workers use bricks, concrete and concrete blocks, and natural and manmade stones to build structures. Sheet metal workers fabricate or install products that are made from thin metal sheets. Solar photovoltaic (PV) installers assemble, set up, and maintain rooftop or other systems that convert sunlight into energy. Flooring installers and tile and stone setters lay and finish carpet, wood, vinyl, tile, and other materials.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Graphic designers create visual concepts, using computer software or by hand, to communicate ideas that inspire, inform, and captivate consumers. They develop the overall layout and production design for applications such as advertisements, brochures, magazines, and reports.  Meet with clients or the art director to determine the scope of a project
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Graphic designers usually need a bachelor’s degree in graphic design or a related field. Candidates for graphic design positions should have a portfolio that demonstrates their creativity and originality.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Many of these workers are employed in specialized design services, publishing, or advertising, public relations, and related services industries.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: graphic designers.    Art directors are responsible for the visual style and images in magazines, newspapers, product packaging, and movie and television productions. Craft and fine artists use a variety of materials and techniques to create art for sale and exhibition. Desktop publishers use computer software to design page layouts for items that are printed or published online. Drafters use software to convert the designs of engineers and architects into technical drawings. Industrial designers combine art, business, and engineering to develop the concepts for manufactured products. Special effects artists and animators create images that appear to move and visual effects for various forms of media and entertainment. Technical writers prepare instruction manuals, how-to guides, journal articles, and other supporting documents to communicate complex and technical information more easily. Web developers create and maintain websites. Digital designers develop, create, and test website or interface layout, functions, and navigation for usability.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Grounds maintenance workers install and maintain landscapes, prune trees or shrubs, and do other tasks to ensure that vegetation is attractive, orderly, and safe.  Mow, edge, and fertilize lawns Landscaping workers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Grounds maintenance workers typically do not need a formal educational credential and are trained on the job. States may require licensing for workers who apply pesticides or fertilizers.   Ability to work at heights.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most grounds maintenance work is done outdoors in all weather conditions. Some work is seasonal, available mainly in the spring, summer, and fall. The work may be repetitive and physically demanding, requiring frequent bending, kneeling, lifting, or shoveling.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: grounds maintenance workers.    Agricultural workers maintain crops and tend livestock. Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers run establishments that produce crops, livestock, and dairy products. Forest and conservation workers perform physical labor to improve the quality of natural areas such as forests, rangelands, and wetlands. Janitors and building cleaners keep many types of buildings clean, sanitary, orderly, and in good condition. Landscape architects design parks and other outdoor spaces. Logging workers harvest forests to provide the raw material for many consumer goods and industrial products. Pest control workers remove insects, rodents, and other pests that infest buildings and surrounding areas.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Hand laborers and material movers manually move freight, stock, or other materials. Some of these workers feed or remove material to or from machines, clean vehicles, pick up unwanted household goods, and pack materials for moving.  Manually move material from one place to another Cleaners of vehicles and equipment
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: There are usually no formal educational requirements to become a hand laborer or material mover. Employers typically require only that applicants be physically able to perform the work.   Customer-service skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most hand laborers and material movers work full time. Because materials are shipped around the clock, some workers, especially those in warehousing, work overnight shifts.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: hand laborers and material movers.    Construction laborers and helpers perform tasks, such as using, supplying, or holding materials or tools and cleaning work areas and equipment, on construction sites. Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers pick up, transport, and drop off packages and small shipments within a local region or urban area. Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers transport goods from one location to another. Material moving machine operators use equipment to transport objects. Material recording clerks track product information in order to keep businesses and supply chains on schedule. Water transportation workers operate and maintain vessels that take cargo and people over water.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Hazardous materials (hazmat) removal workers identify and dispose of harmful substances, such as asbestos, lead, mold, and radioactive waste. They also neutralize and clean up materials that are flammable, corrosive, or toxic.  Follow safety procedures before, during, and after cleanup Asbestos abatement workers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Hazardous materials (hazmat) removal workers typically need a high school diploma and are trained on the job. They must complete training that follows federal, state, and local standards.  Be at least 18 years old Decision-making skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Work environments for hazmat removal workers vary. Completing projects may require night and weekend work. Overtime is common for some workers, particularly for those who respond to emergencies or disasters.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: hazardous materials removal workers.    Construction laborers and helpers perform tasks, such as using, supplying, or holding materials or tools and cleaning work areas and equipment, on construction sites. Firefighters control and put out fires and respond to emergencies involving life, property, or the environment. Insulation workers install and replace the materials used to insulate buildings or mechanical systems. Water and wastewater treatment plant and system operators manage a system of machines to transfer or treat water or wastewater.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Health and safety engineers apply their knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, psychology, and other disciplines to promote worksite or product safety.  Apply knowledge of current policies, regulations, and industrial processes related to health and safety fire prevention and protection engineers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Health and safety engineers typically need a bachelor’s degree in engineering or a related field to enter the occupation. Completing internships or cooperative-education programs may be helpful for gaining hands-on experience while in school.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Health and safety engineers typically work in an office setting, and most are full time. They also may need to travel to worksites.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: health and safety engineers.    Construction and building inspectors ensure that construction meets building codes and ordinances, zoning regulations, and contract specifications. Fire inspectors detect fire hazards, recommend prevention measures, ensure compliance with state and local fire regulations, and investigate causes of fires. Industrial engineers design, develop, and test integrated systems for managing industrial production processes. Mining and geological engineers design mines to safely and efficiently remove minerals for use in manufacturing and utilities. Occupational health and safety specialists and technicians collect data on, analyze, and design improvements to work environments and procedures.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Health education specialists teach people about behaviors that promote wellness. They develop strategies to improve the well-being of individuals and communities.  Assess the health needs of individuals and communities healthcare facilities
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Health education specialists typically need at least bachelor’s degree. Some employers require or prefer that health education specialists be certified.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Health education specialists are employed in a variety of settings, including hospitals, nonprofit organizations, and government agencies. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: health education specialists.    Community health workers promote wellness by helping people adopt healthy behaviors. They implement programs and advocate for people who may have limited access to health resources and social services. Dietitians and nutritionists plan and conduct food service or nutritional programs to help people lead healthy lives. Epidemiologists are public health workers who investigate patterns and causes of disease and injury. High school teachers teach academic lessons and various skills that students will need to attend college and to enter the job market. Middle school teachers educate students, typically in sixth through eighth grades. Postsecondary teachers instruct students in a variety of academic subjects beyond the high school level. School counselors help students develop academic and social skills. Career counselors and advisors help people choose a path to employment. Social and human service assistants provide client services in a variety of fields, such as psychology, rehabilitation, and social work. Social workers help people prevent and cope with problems in their everyday lives. Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors advise people on a range of issues, such as those relating to alcoholism, addictions, or depression. Marriage and family therapists diagnose and treat cognitive, behavioral, or similar disorders in the context of couples and other relationships.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Health Information Technologist or Medical Registrar
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Health information technologists and medical registrars advise organizations on computerized healthcare systems and analyze clinical data.  Help to determine requirements for computerized healthcare systems Health information technologists
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Education requirements for health information technologists and medical registrars vary. Some workers typically need an associate’s degree; others may need a bachelor’s or higher degree. Certification may be required or preferred.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Health information technologists and medical registrars usually work in an office setting and may spend many hours at a computer. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: health information technologists and medical registrars.     Medical assistants complete administrative and clinical tasks, such as scheduling appointments and taking patients’ vital signs. Medical records specialists compile, process, and maintain patient files. Medical transcriptionists use electronic devices to convert voice recordings from physicians and other healthcare workers into formal reports.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Heating, Air Conditioning, or Refrigeration Mechanic and Installer
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers work on heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration (HVACR) systems that control the temperature and air quality in buildings.  Install, maintain, and repair HVACR systems HVAC technicians
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers (HVAC technicians) typically need a postsecondary nondegree award, although some enter the occupation with less education. Once hired, they typically have a lengthy period of on-the-job training to attain competency. HVAC technicians may need a license or certification.   Customer-service skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: These workers install and repair systems in homes, schools, hospitals, and other buildings. They may need to work in cramped spaces, outdoors, or in extreme temperatures. Most work full time, and schedules may vary.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers.    Boilermakers assemble, install, maintain, and repair boilers, closed vats, and other large vessels or containers that hold liquids and gases. Electricians install, maintain, and repair electrical power, communications, lighting, and control systems. Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters install and repair piping fixtures and systems. Sheet metal workers fabricate or install products that are made from thin metal sheets. Solar photovoltaic (PV) installers assemble, set up, and maintain rooftop or other systems that convert sunlight into energy. General maintenance and repair workers fix and maintain machines, mechanical equipment, and buildings. Wind turbine service technicians maintain and repair wind turbines. Stationary engineers and boiler operators control stationary engines, boilers, or other mechanical equipment.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers transport goods from one location to another. Most tractor-trailer drivers are long-haul drivers and operate trucks with a total weight exceeding 26,000 pounds for the vehicle, passengers, and cargo. These drivers deliver goods over intercity routes that sometimes span several states.  Drive long distances owner-operators
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers usually have a high school diploma and attend a professional truck driving school. They must have a commercial driver’s license (CDL).   Hand-eye coordination.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Working as a long-haul truck driver is a lifestyle choice because these drivers can be away from home for days or weeks at a time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers.    Bus drivers transport people between various places. Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers pick up, transport, and drop off packages and small shipments within a local region or urban area. Hand laborers and material movers manually move freight, stock, or other materials. Material recording clerks track product information in order to keep businesses and supply chains on schedule. Railroad workers ensure that passenger and freight trains operate safely. They may drive trains, coordinate the activities of the trains, or control signals and switches in the rail yard. Water transportation workers operate and maintain vessels that take cargo and people over water.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Heavy Vehicle or Mobile Equipment Service Technician
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians, also called mechanics, inspect, maintain, and repair vehicles and machinery used in construction, farming, rail transportation, and other industries.  Consult equipment operating manuals, blueprints, and drawings mechanics
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Most heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians have a high school diploma or equivalent. Because vehicle and equipment technology is increasingly sophisticated and computerized, some employers prefer to hire service technicians who have completed a formal training program at a postsecondary institution.   Dexterity.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Service technicians usually work indoors in noisy repair shops. They often lift heavy parts and tools, handle greasy and dirty equipment, and stand or lie in uncomfortable positions. Most service technicians work full time, and many work evenings and weekends.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians.    Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians install, test, adjust, and repair equipment and systems in aircraft. Automotive body and glass repairers restore, refinish, and replace vehicle bodies and frames, windshields, and window glass. Automotive service technicians and mechanics inspect, maintain, and repair cars and light trucks. Diesel service technicians and mechanics inspect, repair, and overhaul buses, trucks, or any vehicle with a diesel engine. Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights install, maintain, and repair factory equipment and other industrial machinery. Small engine mechanics inspect, service, and repair motorized power equipment. Water transportation workers operate and maintain vessels that take cargo and people over water.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: High school teachers help prepare students for life after graduation. They teach academic lessons and various skills that students will need to attend college or to enter the job market.  Plan lessons and instruct their students in the subject they teach
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: High school teachers typically must have at least a bachelor’s degree. In addition, public school teachers must have a state-issued certification or license.  A bachelor’s degree with a minimum grade point average Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: High school teachers work in schools. They work during school hours but may also work evenings and weekends to prepare lessons and grade papers. Most do not teach during the summer.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: high school teachers.    Career and technical education teachers instruct students in various technical and vocational subjects, such as auto repair, healthcare, and culinary arts. Elementary, middle, and high school principals oversee all school operations, including daily school activities. Kindergarten and elementary school teachers instruct young students in basic subjects in order to prepare them for future schooling. Middle school teachers educate students, typically in sixth through eighth grades. Postsecondary teachers instruct students in a variety of academic subjects beyond the high school level. Preschool teachers educate and care for children younger than age 5 who have not yet entered kindergarten. School counselors help students develop academic and social skills. Career counselors and advisors help people choose a path to employment. Special education teachers work with students who have a wide range of learning, mental, emotional, and physical disabilities. Teacher assistants work with a licensed teacher to give students additional attention and instruction. Adult basic and secondary education and ESL (English as a Second Language) teachers instruct adults in fundamental skills, such as reading and speaking English. They also help students earn their high school equivalency credential.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Historians research, analyze, interpret, and write about the past by studying historical documents and sources.  Gather historical data from various sources, including archives, books, and artifacts
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Historians typically need at least a master’s degree to enter the occupation. Those with a bachelor’s degree in history may qualify for some entry-level positions, but most will find jobs in different fields.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Historians must travel to carry out research. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: historians.    Anthropologists and archeologists study the origin, development, and behavior of humans. Archivists and curators oversee institutions’ collections, such as of historical items or of artwork. Museum technicians and conservators prepare and restore items in those collections. Economists conduct research, prepare reports, and evaluate issues related to monetary and fiscal policy. They also may collect and analyze statistical data. Editors plan, review, and revise content for publication. Geographers study the Earth and the distribution of its land, features, and inhabitants. High school teachers teach academic lessons and various skills that students will need to attend college and to enter the job market. Political scientists study the origin, development, and operation of political systems. Postsecondary teachers instruct students in a variety of academic subjects beyond the high school level. Sociologists study society and social behavior by examining the groups, cultures, social institutions, and processes that develop when people interact and work together. Writers and authors develop written content for various types of media.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Home Health or Personal Care Aide
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Home health and personal care aides monitor the condition of people with disabilities or chronic illnesses and help them with daily living activities. They often help older adults who need assistance. Under the direction of a nurse or other healthcare practitioner, home health aides may be allowed to give a client medication or to check the client’s vital signs.  Assist clients in their daily personal tasks, such as bathing or dressing Home health aides
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Home health and personal care aides typically need a high school diploma or equivalent, but some positions do not require it. Those working in certified home health or hospice agencies must complete formal training and pass a standardized test.   Detail oriented.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Home health and personal care aides work in a variety of settings, including clients’ homes, group homes, and day services programs. Most aides work full time, although part-time work is common. Work schedules may vary.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: home health and personal care aides.    Childcare workers attend to children's needs while helping to foster early development. Licensed practical nurses (LPNs) and licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) provide basic medical care. Medical assistants complete administrative and clinical tasks, such as scheduling appointments and taking patients’ vital signs. Nursing assistants provide basic care and help patients with activities of daily living. Orderlies transport patients and clean treatment areas. Occupational therapy assistants and aides help occupational therapists provide treatments and procedures to clients, or they do routine tasks such as preparing treatment rooms. Physical therapist assistants and aides are supervised by physical therapists to help patients regain movement and manage pain after injuries and illnesses. Psychiatric technicians and aides care for people who have mental conditions or developmental disabilities. Registered nurses (RNs) provide and coordinate patient care and educate patients and the public about various health conditions. Social and human service assistants provide client services in a variety of fields, such as psychology, rehabilitation, and social work.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Human resources managers plan, coordinate, and direct the administrative functions of an organization. They oversee the recruiting, interviewing, and hiring of new staff; consult with top executives on strategic planning; and serve as a link between an organization’s management and its employees.  Plan and coordinate an organization’s workforce to best use employees’ talents Labor relations directors
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Candidates typically need a combination of education and several years of related work experience to become a human resources manager. Although most positions require a bachelor’s degree, some require a master’s degree.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Human resources managers are employed in nearly every industry. They work in offices, and most work full time during regular business hours. Some travel to attend professional meetings or to recruit employees.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: human resources managers.    Administrative services and facilities managers plan, direct, and coordinate activities that help an organization run efficiently. Compensation and benefits managers plan, develop, and oversee programs to pay employees. Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists oversee wage and nonwage programs that an organization provides to its employees in return for their work. They also evaluate position descriptions to determine details such as classification and salary. Human resources specialists recruit, screen, and interview job applicants and place newly hired workers in jobs. They also may handle compensation and benefits, training, and employee relations. Labor relations specialists resolve employee-management disputes and negotiate labor contracts. Top executives plan strategies and policies to ensure that an organization meets its goals. Training and development managers plan, coordinate, and direct skills- and knowledge-enhancement programs for an organization’s staff. Training and development specialists plan and administer programs that improve the skills and knowledge of their employees.

/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Human resources specialists typically need a bachelor’s degree to enter the occupation.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Human resources specialists generally work in office settings. /occupation/similar_occupations/section_: human resources specialists.    Compensation and benefits managers plan, develop, and oversee programs to pay employees. /occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Hydrologists study water and how it moves across and through the Earth’s crust. They research the distribution, circulation, and physical properties of surface water and groundwater. They also study the form and intensity of precipitation and its rate of evaporation into the atmosphere, infiltration into soil, or return to the ocean.  Measure streamflow, volume, and other water-cycle elements of bodies of water
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: To enter the occupation, hydrologists typically need a bachelor’s degree in geology, hydrology, or a related field. However, some employers prefer to hire candidates who have a master’s degree.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Hydrologists typically work in an office setting and in the field. They may need to travel to lakes, streams, and other locations and work outdoors in all types of weather. Most hydrologists work full time, and some work more than 40 hours a week.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: hydrologists.    Atmospheric scientists study, report on, and forecast the weather and climate. Civil engineers plan, design, and supervise the construction and maintenance of building and infrastructure projects. Conservation scientists and foresters manage the land quality of forests, parks, rangelands, and other natural resources. Environmental engineers use engineering disciplines in developing solutions to problems of planetary health. Environmental science and protection technicians monitor the environment and investigate sources of pollution and contamination, including those affecting public health. Environmental scientists and specialists conduct research or investigations to protect the environment or human health. Geoscientists study the physical aspects of the Earth. Agricultural engineers solve problems concerning power supplies, machine efficiency, the use of structures and facilities, pollution and environmental issues, and the storage and processing of agricultural products. Geological and hydrologic technicians support scientists and engineers in exploring, extracting, and monitoring natural resources. Mining and geological engineers design mines to safely and efficiently remove minerals for use in manufacturing and utilities.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Industrial designers develop the concepts for manufactured products, such as cars, home appliances, and toys. They combine art, business, and engineering to make products that people use every day. Industrial designers consider the function, aesthetics, production costs, and usability of products when developing new product concepts. /occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Industrial designers typically need a bachelor's degree to enter the occupation. They also need an electronic portfolio with examples of their design projects.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Industrial designers work in a variety of industries. Although industrial designers work primarily in offices, they may travel to testing facilities, design centers, clients’ exhibit sites, users’ homes or workplaces, and places where the product is manufactured.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: industrial designers.    Architects plan and design houses, factories, office buildings, and other structures. Graphic designers create visual concepts, using computer software or by hand, to communicate ideas that inspire, inform, and captivate consumers. Industrial engineers design, develop, and test integrated systems for managing industrial production processes. Interior designers make indoor spaces functional, safe, and beautiful by determining space requirements and selecting essential and decorative items. Art directors are responsible for the visual style and images in magazines, newspapers, product packaging, and movie and television productions. Fashion designers create clothing, accessories, and footwear. Software developers design computer applications or programs. Software quality assurance analysts and testers identify problems with applications or programs and report defects.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians help engineers solve problems affecting manufacturing layout or production. They prepare machinery and equipment plans, design workflows, conduct statistical production studies, and analyze production costs. /occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians typically need an associate’s degree or a postsecondary certificate to enter the occupation. /occupation/summary_work_environment: Most industrial engineering technologists and technicians work in manufacturing industries. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: industrial engineering technologists and technicians. Evaluate manufacturing, delivery, customer experience, or other systems and identify ways to improve productivity and quality Human factors engineers

Quality control inspectors examine products and materials for defects or deviations from specifications.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Industrial Machinery Mechanic, Machinery Maintenance Worker, or Millwright
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Industrial machinery mechanics and machinery maintenance workers maintain and repair factory equipment and other industrial machinery, such as conveying systems, production machinery, and packaging equipment. Millwrights install, dismantle, repair, reassemble, and move machinery in factories, power plants, and construction sites.  Read technical manuals to understand equipment and controls Industrial machinery mechanics
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights typically need a high school diploma. Industrial machinery mechanics and machinery maintenance workers also usually need a year or more of training after high school.  Minimum age of 18 Manual dexterity.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Workers in this occupation must follow safety precautions and use protective equipment, such as hardhats, safety glasses, and hearing protectors. Most work full time in manufacturing facilities. However, they may be on call and work night or weekend shifts. Overtime is common.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights. General maintenance and repair workers fix and maintain machines, mechanical equipment, and buildings. Machinists and tool and die makers set up and operate equipment to produce precision metal parts, instruments, and tools. Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters install and repair piping fixtures and systems. Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers use hand-held or remotely controlled equipment to join, repair, or cut metal parts and products. Wind turbine service technicians maintain and repair wind turbines. Medical equipment repairers install, maintain, and repair patient care equipment.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Industrial production managers oversee the operations of manufacturing and related plants. They coordinate, plan, and direct activities involved in creating a range of goods, such as cars, computer equipment, and paper products.  Decide how best to use a plant’s workers and equipment to meet production goals plant managers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Industrial production managers typically need a bachelor’s degree and several years of related work experience.   Business skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most industrial production managers work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week.

Computer programmers write, modify, and test code and scripts that allow computer software and applications to function properly. Computer support specialists maintain computer networks and provide technical help to computer users. Computer systems analysts study an organization’s current computer systems and design ways to improve efficiency. /occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Most floor, ceiling, and wall insulators learn their trade on the job. Many mechanical insulators complete an apprenticeship program after earning a high school diploma or equivalent.   Ability to work at heights.

/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: insurance sales agents. Technical writers prepare instruction manuals, how-to guides, journal articles, and other supporting documents to communicate complex and technical information more easily. Writers and authors develop written content for various types of media.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Ironworkers install structural and reinforcing iron and steel to form and support bridges, roads, and other structures.  Read and follow blueprints, sketches, and other instructions erectors
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Most ironworkers learn through an apprenticeship or on-the-job training.   Ability to work at heights.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Ironworkers perform physically demanding and dangerous work, often at great heights. Workers must wear safety equipment to reduce the risk of falls or other injuries.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: ironworkers.    Assemblers and fabricators build finished products and the parts that go into them. Boilermakers assemble, install, maintain, and repair boilers, closed vats, and other large vessels or containers that hold liquids and gases. Carpenters construct, repair, and install building frameworks and structures made from wood and other materials. Construction laborers and helpers perform tasks, such as using, supplying, or holding materials or tools and cleaning work areas and equipment, on construction sites. Masonry workers use bricks, concrete and concrete blocks, and natural and manmade stones to build structures. Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers use hand-held or remotely controlled equipment to join, repair, or cut metal parts and products.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Janitors and building cleaners keep many types of buildings clean, sanitary, orderly, and in good condition.  Gather and empty trash Building superintendents
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Janitors and building cleaners typically do not need formal education to enter the occupation. However, some employers may require or prefer that workers have a high school diploma or equivalent. Most janitors and building cleaners learn on the job.   Interpersonal skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Janitors and building cleaners usually work indoors, but they may also work outdoors on tasks such as sweeping walkways or removing snow. Most janitors and building cleaners work full time, although part-time work is common. Work schedules may vary to include evenings, nights, or weekends.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: janitors and building cleaners.    Grounds maintenance workers install and maintain landscapes, prune trees or shrubs, and do other tasks to ensure that vegetation is attractive, orderly, and safe. Pest control workers remove insects, rodents, and other pests that infest buildings and surrounding areas.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Jeweler or Precious Stone and Metal Worker
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers design, construct, adjust, repair, appraise and sell jewelry and related products.  Design and create jewelry from precious metals and stones Bench jewelers,
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers typically need a high school diploma to enter the occupation, and they learn their skills on the job. Some workers complete an apprenticeship or trade school program.   Creativity.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers may spend much of their time at a workbench or polishing station, using tools and chemicals. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: jewelers and precious stone and metal workers.    Craft and fine artists use a variety of materials and techniques to create art for sale and exhibition. Fashion designers create clothing, accessories, and footwear. Industrial designers combine art, business, and engineering to develop the concepts for manufactured products. Retail sales workers sell merchandise, spare and replacement parts, and equipment to customers. Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers use hand-held or remotely controlled equipment to join, repair, or cut metal parts and products. Woodworkers manufacture a variety of products, such as cabinets and furniture, using wood, veneers, and laminates.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Judges and hearing officers oversee legal matters in court or administrative proceedings. They may conduct pretrial hearings, facilitate negotiations between opposing parties, and issue legal decisions.  Research legal issues Judges, magistrate judges, and magistrates
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Judges and hearing officers typically need a law degree and work experience as a lawyer. However, specific requirements may vary.   Analytical skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Judges and hearing officers are employed by the federal government or by local and state governments. Most judges and hearing officers work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: judges and hearing officers.    Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators facilitate negotiation through dialogue to help resolve conflicts outside of the court system. Lawyers advise and represent clients on legal proceedings or transactions. Paralegals and legal assistants supportlawyersby performing a variety of tasks, such as maintaining and organizing files, conducting legal research, and drafting documents. Private detectives and investigators gather, analyze, and report information to clients regarding legal or personal matters.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers instruct young students in basic subjects, such as math and reading, in order to prepare them for middle school.  Create lesson plans to teach students subjects, such as reading, science, and math English as a second language (ESL)
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers usually must have a bachelor’s degree. In addition, public school teachers must have a state-issued certification or license.  A bachelor’s degree with a minimum grade point average Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers work in public and private schools. They generally work during school hours when students are present and use nights and weekends to prepare lessons and grade papers. Most kindergarten and elementary school teachers do not work during the summer.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: kindergarten and elementary school teachers.    Career and technical education teachers instruct students in various technical and vocational subjects, such as auto repair, healthcare, and culinary arts. Childcare workers attend to children's needs while helping to foster early development. Elementary, middle, and high school principals oversee all school operations, including daily school activities. High school teachers teach academic lessons and various skills that students will need to attend college and to enter the job market. Instructional coordinators oversee school curriculums and teaching standards. They develop instructional material, implement it, and assess its effectiveness. Librarians and library media specialists help people find information and conduct research for personal and professional use. Career counselors and advisors help people choose a path to employment. Social workers help people prevent and cope with problems in their everyday lives. Special education teachers work with students who have a wide range of learning, mental, emotional, and physical disabilities. Teacher assistants work with a licensed teacher to give students additional attention and instruction.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Labor relations specialists (also called employee relations specialists) resolve employee-management disputes, negotiate labor contracts, and coordinate grievance procedures regarding worker complaints. They may offer input on issues such as wages and salaries, nonwage benefits, and union or management practices.  Support interactions and negotiations between management and employee representatives, such as labor unions
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: To enter the occupation, these specialists typically need a bachelor’s degree in labor and industrial relations, human resources, business, or a related field. Specialists also may need several years of experience in a related occupation.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Labor relations specialists typically work in an office setting. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: labor relations specialists.    Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators facilitate negotiation through dialogue to help resolve conflicts outside of the court system. Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists oversee wage and nonwage programs that an organization provides to its employees in return for their work. They also evaluate position descriptions to determine details such as classification and salary. Human resources managers plan, coordinate, and direct the administrative functions of an organization. Human resources specialists recruit, screen, and interview job applicants and place newly hired workers in jobs. They also may handle compensation and benefits, training, and employee relations. Lawyers advise and represent clients on legal proceedings or transactions. Public relations specialists create and maintain a positive public image for the clients they represent. Training and development managers plan, coordinate, and direct skills- and knowledge-enhancement programs for an organization’s staff. Training and development specialists plan and administer programs that improve the skills and knowledge of their employees. Social and human service assistants provide client services in a variety of fields, such as psychology, rehabilitation, and social work.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Landscape architects design parks and the outdoor spaces of campuses, recreational facilities, businesses, private homes, and other open spaces.  Meet with clients, engineers, and building architects to understand the requirements of a project
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Landscape architects usually need at least a bachelor’s degree in landscape architecture and a state-issued license, which typically requires completion of an internship.   Analytical skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Landscape architects spend much of their time in offices, where they create designs, prepare models, and meet with clients. They spend the rest of their time at jobsites.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: landscape architects.    Architects plan and design houses, factories, office buildings, and other structures. Civil engineers plan, design, and supervise the construction and maintenance of building and infrastructure projects. Construction managers plan, coordinate, budget, and supervise construction projects from start to finish. Environmental scientists and specialists conduct research or investigations to protect the environment or human health. Hydrologists study water and how it moves across and through the Earth’s crust. Surveying and mapping technicians collect data and make maps of the Earth's surface. Surveyors make precise measurements to determine property boundaries. Urban and regional planners develop comprehensive plans and programs for use of land and physical facilities in cities, counties, metropolitan areas, and other jurisdictions. Drafters use software to convert the designs of engineers and architects into technical drawings. Interior designers make indoor spaces functional, safe, and beautiful by determining space requirements and selecting essential and decorative items.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Lawyers advise and represent clients on legal proceedings or transactions.  Advise and represent clients in criminal or civil proceedings and in other legal matters attorneys
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Lawyers typically need a law degree and a state license, which usually requires passing a bar examination.   Analytical skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Lawyers work for a variety of organizations, usually in office settings. Some work for federal, local, or state governments. Most work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: lawyers.    Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators facilitate negotiation through dialogue to help resolve conflicts outside of the court system. /occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Librarians typically need a master’s degree in library science (MLS). School librarians and library media specialists typically need a bachelor’s or master’s degree in a related field, along with a teaching certificate; requirements vary by state.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Librarians and library media specialists work for local governments, schools, and other organizations. Most work full time, although part-time work is common.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: librarians and library media specialists. Museum technicians and conservators prepare and restore items in those collections. Instructional coordinators oversee school curriculums and teaching standards. They develop instructional material, implement it, and assess its effectiveness. Kindergarten and elementary school teachers instruct young students in basic subjects in order to prepare them for future schooling. Library technicians and assistants help librarians with all aspects of running a library. Middle school teachers educate students, typically in sixth through eighth grades. Postsecondary teachers instruct students in a variety of academic subjects beyond the high school level.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Library technicians and assistants help librarians with all aspects of running a library. They assist patrons, organize library materials and information, and do clerical and administrative tasks.  Loan library materials to patrons and collect returned materials Academic library technicians and assistants
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Library technicians typically need a postsecondary certificate. Library assistants typically need a high school diploma or its equivalent, combined with short-term on-the-job training.   Communication skills.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Library technicians and assistants work in local public libraries, corporate and specialty libraries, and school and university libraries.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: library technicians and assistants.    Librarians and library media specialists help people find information and conduct research for personal and professional use. Medical records specialists compile, process, and maintain patient files. Receptionists do tasks such as answering phones, receiving visitors, and providing information about their organization to the public. Teacher assistants work with a licensed teacher to give students additional attention and instruction.

/occupation/occupation_name_short_singul: Licensed Practical or Licensed Vocational Nurse
/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Licensed practical nurses (LPNs) and licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) provide basic medical care to ill, injured, or convalescing patients or to persons with disabilities. Responsibilities for LPNs and LVNs are nearly identical; their title depends on the state in which they work.  Monitor patients’ health by checking their blood pressure, body temperature, and other vital signs
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Licensed practical nurses (LPNs) and licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) must complete a state-approved educational program, which typically takes about 1 year. They also must have a license.   Compassion.
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses work in a variety of settings, including nursing and residential care facilities, hospitals, physicians’ offices, and private homes. Most work full time.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses.    Nursing assistants provide basic care and help patients with activities of daily living. Orderlies transport patients and clean treatment areas. Occupational therapy assistants and aides help occupational therapists provide treatments and procedures to clients, or they do routine tasks such as preparing treatment rooms. Physical therapist assistants and aides are supervised by physical therapists to help patients regain movement and manage pain after injuries and illnesses. Psychiatric technicians and aides care for people who have mental conditions or developmental disabilities. Registered nurses (RNs) provide and coordinate patient care and educate patients and the public about various health conditions. Surgical assistants and technologists help with surgical operations. Medical assistants complete administrative and clinical tasks, such as scheduling appointments and taking patients’ vital signs.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Loan officers evaluate, authorize, or recommend approval of applications for personal and business loans.  Contact businesses or people to ask if they need a loan Commercial loan officers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: Loan officers typically need a bachelor’s degree and on-the-job training. Mortgage loan officers must be licensed.   Decision-making skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most loan officers are employed by commercial banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, and other financial institutions. Most loan officers work full time, and some work more than 40 hours per week. Except for consumer loan officers, who spend most of their time in offices, these workers may travel to visit clients.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: loan officers.    Financial analysts guide businesses and individuals in decisions about expending money to attain profit. Financial examiners ensure compliance with laws that govern institutions handling monetary transactions. Personal financial advisors provide advice to help individuals manage their money and plan for their financial future. Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents determine how much is owed in taxes and collect tax from individuals and businesses on behalf of the government. Insurance sales agents contact potential customers and sell one or more types of insurance. Securities, commodities, and financial services sales agents connect buyers and sellers in financial markets. Real estate brokers and sales agents help clients buy, sell, and rent properties. Financial managers create financial reports, direct investment activities, and develop plans for the long-term financial goals of their organization. Tellers process routine transactions, such as cashing checks and depositing money, at a bank or credit union.

/occupation/what_they_do/section_body: Lodging managers ensure that guests have a pleasant experience at a hotel, motel, or other type of facility with accommodations. Lodging managers also plan, direct, or coordinate activities to ensure that the facility is efficient and profitable.  Inspect guest rooms, public areas, and grounds for cleanliness and appearance Convention service managers
/occupation/how_to_become_one/section_bo: To enter the occupation, lodging managers typically take one of three paths: a high school diploma combined with several years of experience working in a lodging facility, a bachelor’s degree in hospitality or hotel management, or an associate’s degree or certificate in hotel management.   Business skills
/occupation/summary_work_environment: Most lodging managers work full time. Work schedules may vary and often include evenings, weekends, and holidays. Because these facilities are open around the clock, some managers are on call 24 hours a day.
/occupation/similar_occupations/section_: lodging managers. Gambling services workers serve customers in gambling establishments, such as casinos or racetracks. Human resources managers plan, coordinate, and direct the administrative functions of an organization. Property, real estate, and community association managers oversee many aspects of residential, commercial, or industrial properties. Sales managers plan, direct, or coordinate the delivery of a product or service to the customer.
